# Daytona review, pricing and verdict

Sandboxed cloud computers for running AI agents and AI-written code.

Best for

AI agent engineer

Not for

Team that needs one flat monthly price

By Damien, Founder and editor

What it is

Cloud platforms · GPU clouds

Billing

Pay as you go

Regions

US · Europe

Compliance

SOC 2 · HIPAA

Checked

4 Oct 2026

## Should you use Daytona?

Daytona suits teams building agents that execute generated code and want one vendor for CPU, Windows and GPU sandboxes. The catch is governance: core development went private in June 2026 and the public repository was archived in October. Verdict: use the hosted service, and do not plan around self-hosting.

One account covers CPU sandboxes, Windows desktops and eight GPU models, all metered by the second.

Integrations such as the OpenClaw install docs and a SOC 2 and HIPAA paper trail create some stickiness, but sandboxes are easy to swap between vendors and the archived open source core removes the self-host fallback.

### Also for

- Platform engineer adding code execution to a product
- Engineers building agents that write and run code

Show 3 more

- Platform teams adding safe code execution to a product
- Startups applying for infrastructure credits
- Regulated teams that need SOC 2 or HIPAA paperwork

### Also not for

- Team that must self-host a maintained open source stack

Main trade-off

The open source core is frozen and archived, so anyone who wanted to self-host a maintained platform has to rely on the hosted service.

Billing

Pay as you go

How the pricing works, in full

Billing is per second and metered by resource. Compute is $0.0504 per vCPU-hour, memory is $0.0162 per GiB-hour, and storage is $0.000108 per GiB-hour after the first 5 GiB. Windows sandboxes add $0.0858 per vCPU-hour. GPUs are listed per hour as preemptible or on-demand: RTX 4090 $0.57 or $0.99, RTX 5090 $0.74 or $1.29, RTX PRO 6000 $1.74 or $3.03, H100 $2.27 or $3.95, H200 $2.61 or $4.54, MI355X $3.44 or $5.99, B200 $3.59 or $6.25, B300 $4.08 or $6.25. New accounts get $200 in free compute with no card required, and startups can apply for up to $50k in credits. Enterprise terms (larger limits, SSO, audit logs, bring your own compute) are quoted by sales. Rates read from daytona.io/pricing on 2026-10-04.

### Costs that are easy to miss

- Storage beyond the first 5 GiB is metered per GiB-hour
- Windows sandboxes add a per-vCPU surcharge
- Higher organization limits require top-ups of $25, $500 or $2,000 every 30 days by tier

## What Daytona does

Daytona is a hosted sandbox platform that gives AI agents isolated cloud computers, each with its own kernel, filesystem and network stack. The company says sandboxes start in under 90 milliseconds. It runs in two shared regions, United States and Europe, lists eight GPU models, and publishes SOC 2 Type I and HIPAA documents.

- Per-second metering

Compute, memory and storage are each metered by the second, so a sandbox that runs for 90 seconds is billed for 90 seconds.
- Fast starts (vendor claim)

The company says sandboxes reach code execution in under 90 milliseconds; Hokai has not benchmarked this figure.
- Container and VM sandboxes

VM sandboxes (Linux and Windows) release disk quota when stopped or paused, while stopped container sandboxes keep it until archived.
- Snapshots, builder and volumes

The platform docs list environment snapshots, a declarative image builder and volumes for starting new sandboxes from a saved state.

Show all 6 features

- Eight GPU models

The pricing page lists GPUs from the RTX 4090 to the B300, each offered as preemptible or on-demand capacity.
- Five SDKs plus API, CLI and MCP

Python, TypeScript, Ruby, Go and Java SDKs sit beside a REST API, a command line and an MCP server for agent tools.

## Strengths and limits

### Strengths

- Billing follows actual run time, which suits agents that start many short sandboxes, and the public pricing page lists usage rates only.
- CPU sandboxes, Windows desktops and GPUs come from one vendor, so an agent that needs a model run or a desktop session does not need a second provider.
- Regulated buyers can request audit paperwork from the trust center, which shortens security review.

### Limits

- Core development moved to a private codebase in June 2026 and the public AGPL-3.0 repository was archived on 3 October 2026, so a self-hosted copy gets no fixes.
- Self-serve Tier 1 caps an organization at 10 vCPU and 30 GiB of storage, and Tier 2 needs a linked card and a $25 top-up.
- Only two shared regions (United States and Europe) are listed, so teams in Asia-Pacific need a dedicated or custom region arranged with the vendor.
